summary.text: A 63-year-old man with a past medical history of mitral regurgitation presented to the emergency department with three weeks of fevers measured at 103.0 degrees Fahrenheit nightly, persisting without an identified source despite earlier outside evaluations. He denied recent dental work, colonoscopy, IV drug use, alcohol use, hemodialysis and previous valvular replacement but endorsed vigorous flossing with bloody gingivae; review of systems was otherwise unremarkable and examination found no murmur, skin lesions or nodules.

Initial vitals, electrocardiogram and chest radiograph were normal. White blood cell count was 10,100 cells/uL with an elevated C-reactive protein of 14.00 mg/dL and erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 95 mm/h; complete metabolic panel, urinalysis and thyroid stimulating hormone were within normal limits. Three blood cultures grew Gram-positive cocci speciated to Streptococcus gordonii. After an unremarkable transthoracic echocardiogram, transesophageal echocardiography showed a small vegetation on the posterior leaflet of the mitral valve; the case is reported as subacute S. gordonii infective endocarditis on a native mitral valve.

He was empirically started on intravenous vancomycin and piperacillin/tazobactam, then antibiotics were narrowed by sensitivities to gentamicin every 24 hours and continuous penicillin G. On hospital day three blood cultures no longer grew S. gordonii and he was discharged home on two weeks of outpatient gentamicin and four weeks of penicillin infusions.

ambiguities.description: The abstract and introduction attribute the endocarditis to vigorous flossing ("secondary to vigorous flossing", "flossing-induced"); this is the authors' causal claim for the case, not a tested mechanism, so no cause is recorded on the diagnosis. Do not infer other portals of entry were excluded beyond the denied dental work and procedures.
